title: Cerastae et Propoetides
titleEn: The Horned Men and the Stone Women — Metamorphoses X.220–242
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Orpheus turns to Amathus and tells of two punishments on Venus' island: the Cerastae, who slaughtered their guests on an altar of Jupiter the guest-god and whom Venus turned into bullocks rather than abandon her cities, and the Propoetides, who denied that she was a goddess and whom her anger drove to prostitute themselves before shame left them and they hardened into flint.

sentences.t:
At si forte roges fecundam Amathunta metallis,
an genuisse velit Propoetidas, abnuat aeque
atque illos, gemino quondam quibus aspera cornu
frons erat: unde etiam nomen traxere Cerastae.
sentences.l: But if by chance you should ask Amathus, rich in ores, whether she would wish to have borne the Propoetides, she would deny it just as much as [she would deny having borne] those men whose brow was once rough with a twin horn: from which they also drew the name Cerastae.
sentences.i: But if you happened to ask Amathus, rich in her ores, whether she would want to have given birth to the Propoetides, she would deny it — and deny just as flatly that she bore those men whose foreheads were once rough with a pair of horns, and who took their very name from them: the Cerastae.
sentences.n: Amathus is a city on the south coast of Cyprus, personified here and put a question as though it were a person; Amathunta is the Greek accusative of its name, and metallis is an ablative of respect with fecundam, “rich in ores.” roges and abnuat are both potential subjunctives — “should you ask … she would deny” — with an genuisse velit an indirect question held inside them. aeque atque means “just as much as,” and the literal supplies in brackets the verb Latin lets the reader carry over to illos. In the relative clause quibus is a dative of possession, “to whom the brow was rough”; gemino … cornu is singular where English wants a pair. traxere is traxerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect, and you will meet the form again in this part; Cerastae is Greek for “the horned ones.”

sentences.t: Ante fores horum stabat Iovis Hospitis ara;
sentences.l: Before the doors of these men stood an altar of Jupiter the Guest-God;
sentences.i: In front of their doors there stood an altar to Jupiter, protector of guests;
sentences.n: horum is a genitive plural, “of these men,” depending on fores — not an adjective agreeing with the doors. Iuppiter Hospes is Jupiter in the office of guest-protector: the god who guarantees the bond between a host and the stranger he takes in. An altar to that god standing at the door is exactly where an arriving guest would read a promise of safety, and the next unit says what was actually killed on it.

sentences.t:
ignarus sceleris quam siquis sanguine tinctam
advena vidisset, mactatos crederet illic
lactantes vitulos Amathusiacasque bidentes:
hospes erat caesus.
sentences.l: And this altar — if any stranger ignorant of the crime had seen it stained with blood, he would believe that suckling calves and Amathusian sheep had been slaughtered there: a guest had been slaughtered.
sentences.i: And if any stranger who knew nothing of the crime had seen that altar stained with blood, he would suppose that suckling calves and the sheep of Amathus had been killed there: what had been killed was a guest.
sentences.n: quam is a connecting relative reaching back to ara — “and this altar” — and it is hauled to the front of its own clause, ahead of the si that governs the verb, with ignarus sceleris pushed further forward still and advena, the noun those two words describe, not arriving until the following line; the literal untangles all of it. vidisset with crederet makes an unreal condition of mixed tense: had he seen it, he would believe. mactatos [esse] is accusative and infinitive after crederet. bidentes are sacrificial sheep, named from their teeth — “two-toothers” — and mactare and caedere are both the vocabulary of sacrifice, so the picture is of ordinary offerings until the colon says what the victim was.

sentences.t:
Sacris offensa nefandis
ipsa suas urbes Ophiusiaque arva parabat
deserere alma Venus.
sentences.l: Offended by unspeakable rites, she herself was preparing to abandon her own cities and the Ophiusian fields — fostering Venus.
sentences.i: Venus the nurturer herself, offended by rites too foul to name, was making ready to abandon her own cities and the fields of Ophiusa.
sentences.n: offensa is a perfect participle taking the ablative sacris nefandis, “offended by” them; nefandus is literally “not to be spoken,” which is why the idiomatic gives “too foul to name.” alma, “nourishing, fostering,” is Venus' standing epithet and it sits pointedly beside those rites. Ophiusa is an old name for Cyprus, so the Ophiusian fields are the island's own, and the cities are suae because Cyprus belonged to her. ipsa, part of the subject, comes early, at the head of its line; only the name itself is held back, to the last two words of the sentence and after both verbs, parabat and deserere. The literal keeps that by ending on the name.

sentences.t:
“Sed quid loca grata, quid urbes
peccavere meae? Quod” dixit “crimen in illis?
sentences.l: “But in what have my pleasant places done wrong, in what my cities?” she said. “What crime [is] in them?
sentences.i: “But what wrong have my own pleasant places done, or my cities?” she said. “What crime is there in them?
sentences.n: peccavere is peccaverunt, the poetic third-plural perfect again. quid with it is an internal accusative — not “what did they sin?” but “in what respect did they do wrong?” meae is feminine plural and can agree grammatically only with urbes; English cannot hold a possessive back that far, so the literal writes “my” before loca grata as well, extending the sense of the one Latin word to both. The second question has no verb at all, and the literal supplies “is” in brackets. dixit is dropped into the middle of the speech rather than set before it, which is why the quotation breaks off and resumes.

sentences.t:
Exsilio poenam potius gens impia pendat,
vel nece, vel siquid medium est mortisque fugaeque.
sentences.l: Let the impious race pay the penalty rather by exile, or by killing, or — if there is anything midway between death and flight — by that.
sentences.i: Let the godless race pay for it by exile instead, or by killing, or by whatever lies midway between death and flight, if there is such a thing.
sentences.n: pendat is a jussive subjunctive, “let it pay,” and poenam pendere is the ordinary idiom for paying a penalty; exsilio and nece are ablatives of means naming the coin it is paid in. In siquid medium est mortisque fugaeque the two genitives depend on medium — “the midpoint of death and of flight” — where English wants “between,” and the doubled -que … -que couples the two genitives, verse for “both … and.” Venus is bargaining herself down from abandoning the island, and the next unit takes up that middle thing and names it.

sentences.t: Idque quid esse potest, nisi versae poena figurae?”
sentences.l: And what can that be, if not the penalty of a turned form?
sentences.i: And what could that be, if not the punishment of a shape transformed?
sentences.n: Idque picks up the siquid medium of the line before: id is the subject of esse and quid the predicate, “what can that be?” versae figurae is a genitive of definition with poena — the penalty that consists in a form's being turned, not a penalty inflicted on a form. verto, “to turn,” is the verb of the change itself, and it returns in the last line of this part, where the Propoetides are versae into flint. The question is also Venus' answer: asking it is how she decides.

sentences.t:
Dum dubitat, quo mutet eos, ad cornua vultum
flexit et admonita est haec illis posse relinqui:
grandiaque in torvos transformat membra iuvencos.
sentences.l: While she hesitates as to what she should change them into, toward the horns she turned her face and was reminded that these could be left to them: and she transforms their huge limbs into grim bullocks.
sentences.i: While she was still weighing what to turn them into, she turned her gaze to the horns and it came to her that these could be left them — and she transforms their great limbs into grim young bulls.
sentences.n: dum takes a present indicative, dubitat, for an action in past time, and the literal keeps the present. quo mutet eos is an indirect question with a deliberative subjunctive: “into what she was to change them.” haec is neuter plural and picks up cornua from the line before — the horns are the one thing that can stay. Then the tenses move: flexit and admonita est are perfect, transformat present, and the shift into the present drops the reader into the moment of the change. The last line interlocks its words — grandia, then in torvos, then membra, then iuvencos, with transformat standing in the middle — so that each adjective is cut off from its own noun by the other pair, and limbs and bullocks are tangled in the word order as they are in the change.

sentences.t:
Sunt tamen obscenae Venerem Propoetides ausae
esse negare deam.
sentences.l: Yet the filthy Propoetides dared to deny Venus to be a goddess.
sentences.i: The filthy Propoetides, though, dared to deny that Venus was a goddess.
sentences.n: audeo is semi-deponent: sunt … ausae is passive in form and active in meaning, “they dared.” The auxiliary sunt opens the line and its participle ausae closes it, and esse is held over to the following line, so what is being denied is not out until deam. Venerem … esse deam is accusative and infinitive after negare, which the literal keeps as “Venus to be a goddess.” obscenae is the narrator's own word and it is not mild — foul, filthy, ill-omened at once — and he fixes it to the women before he has said what they did. Propoetides is a Greek plural, “the daughters of Propoetus.”

sentences.t:
Pro quo sua, numinis ira,
corpora cum forma primae vulgasse feruntur:
sentences.l: In return for which, by the anger of the divinity, they are said to have been the first to prostitute their own bodies along with their beauty:
sentences.i: In return for that, and by the goddess' own anger, they are said to have been the first to prostitute their bodies, and their beauty with them:
sentences.n: Pro quo is a connecting relative — “and in return for this” — reaching back to the denial. numinis ira is an ablative of cause set in as a parenthesis, and it is the load-bearing phrase: Venus' anger is what drove them, so this is a sentence carried out on them and not a choice they made. The parenthesis is wedged into a possessive that is already broken across the line-end: sua ends 239 and corpora, the noun it agrees with, opens 240, so numinis ira stands between the adjective and its noun and across the break. vulgasse is syncopated for vulgavisse, from vulgus, “the crowd”: to make a thing common property, and of a body the phrase is the plain Latin for prostituting oneself. Both layers keep that word at that force; neither softens it. feruntur is a personal passive — Latin says “they are said to have …” where English prefers “it is said that they …” — and primae is nominative with the subject, “the first women to do it.” Magnus prints cum forma, “along with their beauty”; some editions read cum fama, which would make the thing they threw away with their bodies their good name instead.

sentences.t:
utque pudor cessit sanguisque induruit oris,
in rigidum parvo silicem discrimine versae.
sentences.l: And as shame gave way and the blood of their face hardened, they were turned, with only a small difference, into rigid flint.
sentences.i: And once shame had gone from them and the blood in their faces had set hard, it took only a small difference to turn them into unyielding flint.
sentences.n: pudor cessit and sanguis induruit oris together describe the end of blushing: the blood that rises into a face and then will not rise. oris is genitive singular of os, “of the face,” dependent on sanguis. parvo discrimine is an ablative of attendant circumstance, “with only a small difference.” It is not the ablative of degree of difference, which goes with comparatives and words of comparison, and there is no comparative here at all — versae is a perfect participle. The step from a face that can no longer redden to flint is a short one, and that is the grim point of the ending. versae stands without its auxiliary sunt, which Latin omits freely, and the verb is verto once more, the same word Venus used when she settled on a change of shape as the punishment.
